Why Did the US Enter WWI?
Author Lindsay Brinkmann View bio

US involvement in WWI wasn’t guaranteed initially - explore the reasons why America got involved in the Great War and how the war changed thereafter. Updated: 11/19/2021

American Involvement in WWI: Cause and Effect
Lesson Summary
How did the US get involved in WWI?
From April 1914 to November 1918, the world was consumed by a global conflict of World War I. Great Britain, France, and Russia made up the primary members of the Allies, while Germany, Austria-Hungary, and the Ottoman Empire made up the Central Powers. While the countries of Europe quickly formulated alliances, the United States declared neutrality under the Neutrality Act of 1914. The American public did not support the United States entering into World War I because they believed that it was a European conflict. So, traditionally the United States remained out of European affairs. Secondly, President Woodrow Wilson advocated Moral Diplomacy, a conflict between countries, should be worked out through diplomatic discussions rather than military might.
While the United States advocated neutrality, it was difficult for the United States to remain neutral. Eventually, the United States would enter into World War I in April 1917. The United States' advocacy for neutrality from 1914 to 1917, which meant that it was not well prepared to enter World War I. In June 1916, the United States had passed the National Defense Act, which increased the military and approved the construction of additional warships. The United States military was still significantly smaller than the armies of Europe. As a result, the United States had to quickly mobilize for war. To fund the military, the government sold Liberty Bonds, increased personal and corporate income taxes, and placed taxes on luxury goods. Liberty Bonds allowed the government to generate funds quickly with the promise of paying citizens back over a while. These efforts allowed the US Government to raise $33 billion in two years.
World War I Liberty Bond Poster
To increase the size of the military, the government passed the Selective Service Act (1917) which drafted young men between 21 and 30; this would later be pushed back to ages between 18 and 45. Approximately 2.8 million Americans were entered into the military lottery. In addition, about 2 million men will volunteer for military service. Black Americans also joined the US military during World War I. Approximately 400,000 Black Americans served in segregated units during World War I. Civil Rights leaders, such as W.E.B. DuBois, believed that by serving military, Black Americans had an opportunity to achieve equality because the United States advocated joining the war to fight for the future of democracy and freedom for all people. DuBois believed that the United States would have to recognize the equality of Black Americans due to the advocacy for fighting the war for democracy.

Why did the US enter WWI?
While the United States attempted to main neutral in 1914, the war in Europe continually caused problems for the United States. Initially, American manufacturing increased as a result of trading with both the Allies and the Central Powers. However, economists have found that the United States did have a great trade deal with the Allies compared to the Central powers. Germany, in particular, was eager to keep the United States out of the war because they feared the USA would join the Allies, and it would shift the focus of the war. In 1914, Germany declared the waters around Great Britain to be a war zone and that German U-Boats, submarines, would sink ships trading with their enemies. To keep the United States out of the war, Germany ran advertisements in the United States encouraging Americans to stay out of Europe and off of European ships.
While Germany attempted to keep the United States out of the war, the US entrance into the European conflict was inevitable. April 1917, Woodrow Willson went before Congress and asked them to declare war on Germany stating, "The world must be made safe for democracy." On April 6, 1917, the United States entered World War I on the side of the Allies.
But why did the United States enter World War I if they had initially declared neutrality? Historians suggest that three factors contributed to the United States entering World War I:
Unrestricted submarine warfare
Propaganda campaigns
The Zimmerman Telegram
The sinking of the Lusitania
In 1914, Germany had declared the waters around Great Britain a war zone and would sink any ship trading or assisting their enemies, a practice that became known as unrestricted submarine warefare. On May 7, 1915, Germany sank the British ocean liner, the Lusitania. Onboard were 1,200 passengers, which included 128 Americans. While the death of 128 Americans made the diplomatic relationship strained between the United States and Germany, Woodrow Wilson did not advocate for the US to enter the war. Instead, Wilson advocated that Germany stop unrestricted submarine warfare.
In March 1916, the Germanys sank the Sussex, a French passenger liner, killing several Americans. The relationship between Germany and the United States worsened, but Germany issued the Sussex Pledge, which stated that they would not attack merchant or passenger ships without warning. The Sussex Pledge initially improved the relationships between US and Germany; however, it did not last long. On January 31, 1917, Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare as they hoped it would help bring about the end to the war, resulting in the Central Powers' victory.
Frequently Asked Questions
What are three reasons why the US entered WW1?
The United States' entrance into World War I in 1917 as a result of Germany resuming unrestricted submarine warfare after pledging to stop in 1915.  Next, the Allies' propaganda campaigns in the United States built support for anti-German sentiments by depicting Germans as brutal killers.  Finally, the publication of the Zimmerman Telegram, which requested that Mexico attack the United States and distract it from the war in Europe.
When did the US enter into WW1?
After declaring neutrality in 1914, the United States attempted to remain out of World War I. However, the United States was unable to remain out of the fight and entered World War I in April 1917.
Why did the US wait to get involved in ww1?
In 1914, the United States public had supported remaining neutral because:
1) They believe the conflict was a European problem.
2) Wilson advocated solving problems through diplomatic methods rather than physical violence.

American Involvement in World War I: How the War Changed After America's Entry
Lesson Transcript
Instructor: Clint Hughes
Clint has taught History, Government, Speech Communications, and Drama. He has his master's degree in Instructional Design and Technology.
After struggling for almost three years to remain a neutral country, America officially became involved in World War I in April of 1917. Learn about American involvement in the war, the challenge of building troops and funds, and how the war changed after America's entry. Updated: 09/17/2021
American Involvement in WWI
Now, up until just before the U.S. declared war on April 6th, 1917, the U.S. had desperately tried to stay neutral, but ties to Britain, propaganda, the sinking of ships by German U-boats, and a German attempt in the Zimmermann Note to get Mexico to declare war on the U.S. pushed the U.S. to getting involved. In this lesson, we will look at how the U.S. got the troops and funds for the war, the impact at home, and American involvement in combat and bringing the war to an end.
5:29
136K views
Building Troops & Funds
OK, so U.S. ties to Britain, both culturally and practically, for trade reasons, had set the stage for justification for U.S. entry into the war. When Germany refuses to stop sinking U.S. ships and tries to get Mexico to attack the States, President Woodrow Wilson goes before Congress and requests a declaration of war. But now, how does the nation wage this war?
President Wilson actually opposed a draft, but at the point the U.S. declared war there were fewer than 400,000 troops in the U.S. Army and National Guard together. They were in no way prepared for a major war. So, Congress passed the Selective Service Act on May 18, 1917. The act required men between the ages of 21 and 30 to register for the draft. In time, the age range was expanded to 18 to 45. Over 2.8 million were drafted through the war.
That summer, the new recruits, those drafted and enlisted, reported for training. The military was far from ready for them. The barracks had not been built, so soldiers had to sleep in tents. So few supplies had arrived that the soldiers had to train with sticks instead of rifles and barrels instead of horses!
It wasn't only the troops that had to be raised, it was also the funds. Most of the revenue raised was from taxes, but there was also a huge amount of push for war bonds. War bonds are used by countries to raise money for war. Essentially, they are loan notes taken out by the government from the people. In World War I the U.S. dubbed them Liberty Bonds. Many celebrities, including the likes of Charlie Chaplin, made appearances at huge public rallies selling bonds. The Boy Scouts and Girl Scouts actually had a large campaign to sell bonds. Their slogan was, 'Every scout to save a soldier.'
Not every method of funding the war was so direct. Victory gardens were another campaign meant to help financially. These gardens could lessen the stress the war was having on the food supply. But victory gardens did more than just leave more food for the soldiers; they were also a great morale booster. It gave everyday Americans, even those of little means, a way to do their patriotic duty. Simply by growing their own vegetables, a family could be fighting the war at home.
